summary: Describes version 2 of KeyNote, a trust-management system. It specifies the syntax and meaning of assertions, how action attributes are processed, and the application architecture a KeyNote implementation fits into. It lets policy and credentials decide whether an action is allowed. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: KeyNote is a way of writing security rules that every application can read the same way. Instead of a certificate saying 'this key is called Alice', a KeyNote assertion says 'this key may do this, as long as these conditions hold'. A checker reads the assertions and the request together and returns the answer the application asked for.

subtitle: A trust-management system where a key is bound to what it is allowed to do, rather than to a name

tldr.problem: Security policy is usually scattered: access lists in each application, certificates that bind a key to a name, and code that has to work out what either one permits. There was no single mechanism that worked the same way in every application.
tldr.mechanism: KeyNote replaces that with a shared language for policies and credentials. An assertion says who is authorising whom to do what under which conditions, and a compliance checker evaluates the assertions against the requested action to return a compliance value the application has configured.
tldr.outcome: Policies and credentials use the same syntax and are evaluated the same way, so a policy written for one application carries exactly the same structure as one written for another. The memo is an Informational specification of version 2 of the language.

today: RFC 2704 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It specifies version 2 of the KeyNote assertion language, and the memo says that a later document was to address credential expiration and revocation services, which this one does not provide.

sections.title: What Trust Management Is For
sections.content:
Trust management, introduced in the PolicyMaker system, is a unified approach to specifying and interpreting security policies, credentials and relationships. It allows direct authorization of security-critical actions, and a trust-management system provides standard, general-purpose mechanisms for specifying application security policies and credentials.

The key difference from certificates is what a credential binds. Traditional certificates bind keys to names. Trust-management credentials describe a specific delegation of trust and can bind keys directly to the authorization to perform specific tasks. The approach has advantages over other mechanisms for controlling authorization, especially when security policy is distributed across a network or is otherwise decentralized. It unifies the notions of security policy, credentials, access control and authorization: an application simply asks the compliance checker whether a requested action should be allowed. Policies and credentials are written in standard languages shared by all trust-managed applications, so the security configuration for one application carries exactly the same syntactic and semantic structure as that of another, even when the semantics of the applications themselves are quite different. And because the policies are easy to distribute, it avoids the need for application-specific distributed policy configuration, access control lists, and certificate parsers and interpreters.

A trust-management system has five components. A language for describing actions, which are operations with security consequences that the system is to control. A mechanism for identifying principals, the entities that can be authorized to perform actions. A language for specifying application policies, which govern the actions principals are authorized to perform. A language for specifying credentials, which allow principals to delegate authorization to other principals. And a compliance checker, which provides a service to applications for determining how an action requested by principals should be handled, given a policy and a set of credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is to replace a pile of separate mechanisms with one shared language. An application says what it wants to do, a checker compares that request with the rules and the signed statements it holds, and hands back an answer. The same words work in every application, so rules can be written once and reused.

sections.title: KeyNote Concepts
sections.content:
In KeyNote the authority to perform trusted actions is associated with one or more principals. A principal may be a physical entity, a process in an operating system, a public key, or any other convenient abstraction, and is identified by a string called a Principal Identifier. Sometimes the identifier contains a cryptographic key that the system interprets, for instance to verify a signature; in other cases the structure is opaque to KeyNote.

Principals do two things of interest: they request actions, and they issue assertions. An action is any trusted operation the application places under KeyNote control, and it is described to the compliance checker as a collection of name-value pairs called an action attribute set. An assertion delegates the authorization to perform actions to other principals: it identifies who made it, which other principals are being authorized, and the conditions under which the authorization applies.

The application issues a query with a proposed action attribute set and the identity of the principals requesting it, and KeyNote returns a policy compliance value from an ordered set of possible responses. In the simplest case the value is Boolean, such as reject or approve, but assertions can also select from a range, such as no access, restricted access or full access, and the application configures the ordering from weakest to strongest at query time.

One special principal, with the identifier POLICY, provides the root of trust: it is considered authorized to perform any action. Assertions issued by POLICY are policy assertions, and an application's security policy is a collection of them. When a principal is identified by a public key it can sign assertions and distribute them over untrusted networks; these signed assertions are credentials and play a role similar to traditional certificates. Policies and credentials share the same syntax and are evaluated by the same semantics, so a principal can turn its policy assertions into credentials simply by signing them.

One design principle runs through all of it: assertion monotonicity. The compliance value of an action is always positively derived from assertions made by trusted principals, so removing an assertion never results in a higher compliance value. That means a network failure which prevents credentials from arriving can never cause a dangerous action to be authorised.
sections.plainLanguage: The pieces are: principals, who ask for things and pass on permission; actions, which are the things with security consequences; assertions, which say who is permitting whom to do what under which conditions; and a checker that turns all of that into a single answer. A special principal called POLICY sits at the top and may do anything.

sections.title: Action Attributes
sections.content:
Trusted actions to be evaluated by KeyNote are described by a collection of name-value pairs called the action attribute set, which is passed to the compliance checker with each query. Action attributes are how applications communicate requests to KeyNote, and they are the primary objects on which KeyNote assertions operate.

Each attribute has a name and a value. KeyNote does not interpret the meaning of names and values; they vary from application to application and must be agreed between the people writing the application and the people writing the policies and credentials that will be used with it. Names and values are arbitrary-length strings, and KeyNote guarantees support of attribute names and values up to 2048 characters long. What happens with longer ones is not specified and depends on the implementation, so applications and assertions should avoid depending on them.

Attribute values are inherently untyped and are character strings by default. They may contain any non-NUL ASCII character, and numeric values should be converted to an ASCII text representation by the invoking application, so the number 1234.5 becomes the string 1234.5. Attribute names begin with an alphabetic or underscore character and may be followed by any number of alphanumerics and underscores, and they are case-sensitive.
sections.plainLanguage: The request handed to the checker is a set of name-value pairs. KeyNote does not know what any of them mean: the application decides, and the policy is written against those names. Names and values are plain text, and KeyNote only promises to handle up to 2048 characters.

sections.title: The Assertion Language
sections.content:
An assertion is written as a sequence of sections called fields, each specifying one aspect of its semantics. A field starts with an identifier at the beginning of a line and continues until the next field. The syntax is inspired by the format of RFC822-style message headers, so an assertion is something a person can read, store and send as electronic mail.

There are seven fields. KeyNote-Version names the version of the assertion language the assertion was written under, and should appear first; assertions conforming to this document use the version string 2. Local-Constants adds or overrides action attributes within that assertion only, which is a convenient way to give short names to lengthy cryptographic principal identifiers; attributes defined there override any with the same name passed in the action attribute set, and an attribute initialised more than once makes the whole assertion invalid. Authorizer identifies the principal issuing the assertion, given directly or by reference to the attribute namespace. Licensees identifies the principals being authorized, and more than one can be named, with authorization distributed across several principals using and and threshold constructs. Conditions gives the predicates on the action attribute set under which the authorizer trusts the licensees. Comment carries human-readable text, and Signature carries the signature of the authorizer over the rest of the assertion.

The memo's own example is an email certificate: a certificate authority key as the authorizer, one user key as the licensee, and a condition that the request must be for the email application and for that user's address, so the certificate is valid for email only.
sections.plainLanguage: An assertion looks like a set of email headers, one per meaning: who is speaking, who is being allowed, under what conditions, and the signature. That shape is deliberate, so rules can be read and written by people and travel as ordinary text.

sections.title: How the Compliance Value Is Computed
sections.content:
A query has four parameters: the identifier of the principals requesting the action, the action attribute set, the set of compliance values of interest to the application ordered from minimum to maximum trust, and the policy and credential assertions to include in the evaluation. How these reach the evaluator is up to the application: some may be passed explicitly, others looked up externally, such as credentials fetched from a network-based distribution system, and others requested through a callback.

The compliance value of a query is the principal compliance value of the principal named POLICY, and that in turn is the highest of two things: the direct authorization value of the principal, and the assertion compliance values of all assertions that name the principal in their Authorizer field. The direct authorization value is the maximum trust value if the principal is listed in the query as an authorizer of the action, and the minimum otherwise. The assertion compliance value of an assertion is the lower of its conditions compliance value and its licensee compliance value.

The conditions compliance value is the highest value among all the successful clauses in the conditions section. If no clause succeeds, or the conditions field is empty, it is the minimum trust value; if the field is missing altogether, it is the maximum trust value. Each clause has a test and an optional value separated by an arrow, and a clause without a value counts as the maximum trust value, so a plain test is equivalent to the same test with the maximum value. A clause whose value is not named in the query's ordered set counts as the minimum trust value, and nested clauses are evaluated only if their parent test is true.

The licensee compliance value is calculated by substituting each named principal's own compliance value into the licensees expression and evaluating it. A parenthesised expression has the value of what it encloses; an and expression has the lower of its two values; an or expression has the higher; and a K-of expression has the K-th highest value in its list, counting repeated values with multiplicity. An empty licensees field is the minimum trust value and a missing one is the maximum. With only two possible values these rules reduce exactly to ordinary Boolean logic. The memo also notes that if there are exactly two compliance values the resolution reduces to standard Boolean logic, which is how the familiar case behaves.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is worked out from the top down. POLICY is trusted for everything, and its trust is the best of the assertions that mention it. Each assertion contributes the weaker of two numbers: what its conditions allow, and what its licensees are worth. Conditions take the best matching clause. Licensees use and, or and a K-of construct, which is how a rule can demand two people or three out of five.

sections.title: Architecture, Security and IANA
sections.content:
The memo is careful about where responsibility lies. KeyNote binds keys to predicates describing what the key is authorised to do rather than resolving names, so the infrastructure around it differs from that of a name-based certification scheme. A compliance checker decides, from the policy and credential assertions, whether a proposed action is permitted, but how useful that advice is depends on the application. The action attributes and their values must reflect the application's security requirements accurately, and identifying which attributes to include is perhaps the most important task in integrating KeyNote. The policy must be correct and well formed, in particular trust must be deferred only to principals that should be trusted. And the application itself must be trustworthy: KeyNote does not enforce policy, it only advises the applications that call it, and nothing stops an application from submitting misleading assertions or ignoring the answer altogether.

Choosing the credentials to run a query is also up to the application or to some service outside KeyNote. Even so, inappropriate credentials cannot result in the approval of an illegal action, as long as the policy assertions are correct and the action attribute set is passed correctly. Because KeyNote is monotonic, adding an assertion to a query can never lower the compliance value, while omitting credentials may of course cause legal actions to be disallowed. KeyNote does not itself provide credential revocation services, although a credential can be written to expire after a date by including a date test in the predicate; a future document was to address expiration and revocation services.

Three interface shapes are possible: a standalone application that others call, a library that applications link against, or a local trusted service reached through interprocess communication. On security, the memo says only that trust management is itself a security service and that bugs in, or incorrect use of, a compliance checker implementation could have security implications for the applications that use it. The IANA section names three identifier lists the document asks IANA to maintain: application domain identifiers, which need only be unique strings and are case-sensitive, public key format identifiers such as rsa-hex: and dsa-base64:, which are case-insensitive and need an RFC-style document describing the encoding, and signature algorithm identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: The checker advises; it does not enforce. The application has to describe the request accurately, write correct rules, and then act on the answer, which it could ignore if it chose. Even so, feeding the checker the wrong credentials cannot make an illegal action look legal. And KeyNote has no revocation service of its own, though a credential can be written to expire on a date.

viz.caption: A KEYNOTE ASSERTION, WRITTEN AS MESSAGE HEADERS

data.title: An email certificate assertion
data.code:
KeyNote-Version: 2
Comment: A simple, if contrived, email certificate for user mab
Local-Constants:  ATT_CA_key = "RSA:acdfa1df1011bbac"
                  mab_key = "DSA:deadbeefcafe001a"
Authorizer: ATT_CA_key
Licensees: mab_key
Conditions: ((app_domain == "email")  # valid for email only
          && (address == "mab@research.att.com"));
Signature: "RSA-SHA1:f00f2244"
